blocks.text:
Design a real-time leaderboard for a game or contest with millions of players, where scores update continuously as matches finish, and the system needs to answer three specific questions fast at any moment: what is my exact rank right now, who are the current top hundred players, and who is sitting just above and below me. This is a genuinely different problem from the likes counting system covered earlier in this category. Counting likes only ever needed a single aggregate number per post. A leaderboard needs an entire ordered relationship among potentially millions of players at once, since your rank is only meaningful relative to everyone else's score, and that ordering has to update efficiently every time any one score changes.

The idea that makes this tractable is using a data structure purpose-built for exactly this job, an ordered structure that supports inserting or updating a score and finding anyone's rank in roughly logarithmic time, rather than anything that requires re-sorting or re-scanning the whole player base on every single update.

blocks.text: A player's score should be updatable in real time as they complete matches or earn points. Any player should be able to see their current exact rank. The system should return the current top N players, typically the top hundred, for a global or seasonal display. A player should be able to see a small window of players ranked just above and below them, since seeing your own rank alone is far less motivating than seeing exactly who you are competing against. The system should support many independent leaderboards at once, for example one per game mode, per season, or per region.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter most, and getting the balance between the first two right is most of the design.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter most, and getting the balance between the first two right is most of the design.

blocks.alt: Fast rank queries, high write throughput, read availability at scale, durability, and near real-time freshness

blocks.text: Rank queries have to stay fast no matter how large the player base gets, finding your exact position among a hundred million people cannot mean scanning any meaningful fraction of them. Write throughput matters because score updates arrive continuously and in large volume across an entire active player base. Reads dramatically outnumber writes in practice, since checking the leaderboard happens far more often than any single player's score actually changes, which shapes how this design splits reads and writes across different machines. Durability matters because a crash must never silently erase an already-confirmed score. And freshness only needs to be near real time, a rank that is a few hundred milliseconds behind the absolute latest update is completely fine, a rank that is stale by minutes is not.

blocks.text: A single leaderboard is assumed to comfortably fit in one machine's memory even at very large player counts, a claim worked out with real numbers in section 6, and this design deliberately does not attempt to shard the internal ordered structure of one leaderboard across multiple machines. Instead, the system scales by supporting many independent leaderboards, each with its own dedicated primary and set of read replicas. Reads may lag the absolute latest write by up to a few hundred milliseconds when served from a replica, a trade this design accepts in exchange for spreading heavy read traffic away from the single write path. Basic anti-cheat bounds checking on submitted scores is assumed to be in scope, deeper fraud detection is not.

blocks.text: Say one global leaderboard tracks a hundred million players. Each entry in the ordered structure needs to store a user id, a score, and a handful of internal pointers used for fast ordering, roughly a hundred bytes all in. A hundred million entries at a hundred bytes each comes out to about ten gigabytes, comfortably within the memory of a single large, memory-optimized server, which is exactly the arithmetic behind the assumption in section 5 that one leaderboard does not need internal sharding. Score updates might arrive at fifty thousand per second at peak across the whole player base, each one an operation that takes roughly the logarithm of a hundred million steps, around twenty-seven, to complete, a trivial amount of work for a single machine. Reads, by contrast, could run into millions per minute, since checking the leaderboard is a far more common action than any individual score changing.

blocks.text: Every leaderboard has exactly one primary node holding its live, ordered structure, and every score update for that leaderboard goes to that same primary. The primary asynchronously replicates every change to a set of read replicas, and those replicas, not the primary, serve the overwhelming majority of read traffic, top-N lists, individual rank lookups, and nearby-player queries. A separate anti-cheat check sits ahead of the primary, sanity-checking that a submitted score change is even plausible given the game's own rules before it is allowed to touch the leaderboard at all.

blocks.alt: Score updates pass an anti-cheat check before updating the single primary, which replicates asynchronously to read replicas and persists periodically to durable storage; rank queries are served from replicas and a cached top-N list

blocks.text: The primary's core data structure is a skip list, the same underlying technique real systems like Redis use for exactly this problem. A skip list keeps multiple layered levels of links over the same sorted data, sparse at the top and dense at the bottom, letting an update or a rank lookup skip over large chunks of the structure instead of walking through it one entry at a time.

blocks.text: 7.2 Scaling By Adding Leaderboards, Not By Sharding One
blocks.content: 7.2 Scaling By Adding Leaderboards, Not By Sharding One

blocks.text: This is the single most important architectural decision in the whole design. A hundred million entries already fits comfortably on one machine, from the arithmetic in section 6, so there is no pressing need to split one leaderboard's ordered structure across multiple machines, which would be genuinely difficult anyway since a rank is only meaningful relative to the entire structure's total order. The real scaling axis is horizontal across leaderboards: a new game mode, a new season, or a new region simply gets its own dedicated primary and replicas, entirely independent of every other leaderboard.

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the score update flow above, fast in every normal case because the underlying structure is built for exactly this operation. The workflow worth walking through separately is a player's score changing enough to jump past a large number of other players at once, say from rank fifty thousand into the top hundred after a strong match. The skip list handles this the same way it handles any other update, removing the entry from its old position and reinserting it at the new one, still in roughly logarithmic time regardless of how far the position moved, which is exactly what distinguishes this from a naive approach that would need to shift every entry in between.

blocks.alt: A plausible score change, consistent with what the game's own rules allow, is accepted; an implausibly large or fast change is rejected and flagged for review

blocks.text: Leaderboards specifically attract a particular kind of abuse that a like counter does not: players directly manipulating their own submitted score to cheat their way up the rankings, which is exactly why a bounds check against what is mechanically possible in the game sits ahead of the leaderboard itself, rather than trusting every submitted score at face value.

import random
from typing import Dict, List, Optional


# A single node in the skip list, holding one player's score and a set of
# forward pointers at various levels used to skip ahead quickly.
class SkipListNode:
    def __init__(self, user_id: str, score: int, level: int):
        self.user_id = user_id             # whose entry this is
        self.score = score                    # this player's current score
        self.forward: List[Optional["SkipListNode"]] = [None] * level   # one forward pointer per level this node participates in


# An ordered leaderboard structure supporting update and rank lookup in
# roughly logarithmic time, the same underlying idea Redis uses for its
# sorted sets.
class SkipListLeaderboard:
    MAX_LEVEL = 16   # ceiling on how tall the skip list can grow

    def __init__(self):
        self._head = SkipListNode("", -(2 ** 63), SkipListLeaderboard.MAX_LEVEL)   # sentinel node before every real entry
        self._current_score_by_user: Dict[str, int] = {}                             # userId -> their latest known score
        self._level = 1                                                                 # how many levels are currently in use

    # Updates a player's score, removing any previous entry first so a
    # player's position always reflects only their latest score.
    def update_score(self, user_id: str, new_score: int) -> None:
        previous_score = self._current_score_by_user.get(user_id)   # this player's prior score, if any
        if previous_score is not None:
            self._remove(user_id, previous_score)   # remove the stale entry first
        self._insert(user_id, new_score)                # insert at the position matching the new score
        self._current_score_by_user[user_id] = new_score   # remember this as their current score

    # Returns this player's rank, where rank 1 is the highest score,
    # by counting how many nodes at the bottom level precede them.
    def get_rank(self, user_id: str) -> int:
        score = self._current_score_by_user.get(user_id)   # this player's current score
        if score is None:
            return -1   # not on the leaderboard at all
        current = self._head                                   # start scanning from the sentinel
        rank = 0                                                   # nodes counted so far
        for i in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            while current.forward[i] is not None and self._is_higher_priority(current.forward[i], score, user_id):
                current = current.forward[i]   # advance past this higher-ranked node
                rank += 1                          # count it
        return rank + 1   # this player's own position is one past everyone who outranks them

    def _is_higher_priority(self, node: SkipListNode, target_score: int, target_user_id: str) -> bool:
        # Higher score wins; a tie is broken by whichever user id sorts first,
        # giving a stable, deterministic order for equal scores.
        if node.score != target_score:
            return node.score > target_score   # strictly higher score wins outright
        return node.user_id < target_user_id      # equal scores, alphabetically first user id wins

    def _insert(self, user_id: str, score: int) -> None:
        update: List[Optional[SkipListNode]] = [None] * SkipListLeaderboard.MAX_LEVEL   # last node before the insertion point, per level
        current = self._head                                                               # start scanning from the sentinel
        for i in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            while current.forward[i] is not None and self._is_higher_priority(current.forward[i], score, user_id):
                current = current.forward[i]   # keep advancing while the next node outranks the new entry
            update[i] = current   # remember where this level's insertion point is
        new_level = self._random_level()   # how tall this new node will be
        if new_level > self._level:            # the skip list needs to grow taller
            for i in range(self._level, new_level):
                update[i] = self._head   # new top levels start right after the sentinel
            self._level = new_level         # record the new overall height
        new_node = SkipListNode(user_id, score, new_level)   # the node being inserted
        for i in range(new_level):
            new_node.forward[i] = update[i].forward[i]   # splice in after each level's insertion point
            update[i].forward[i] = new_node

    def _remove(self, user_id: str, score: int) -> None:
        update: List[Optional[SkipListNode]] = [None] * SkipListLeaderboard.MAX_LEVEL   # last node before the target, per level
        current = self._head                                                               # start scanning from the sentinel
        for i in range(self._level - 1, -1, -1):
            while (current.forward[i] is not None
                   and not (current.forward[i].user_id == user_id and current.forward[i].score == score)
                   and self._is_higher_priority(current.forward[i], score, user_id)):
                current = current.forward[i]   # keep advancing until just before the target node
            update[i] = current   # remember where this level's removal point is
        target = update[0].forward[0]   # the node that should be the one to remove
        if target is not None and target.user_id == user_id:
            for i in range(self._level):
                if update[i].forward[i] is not target:
                    break   # this level doesn't reference the target, stop
                update[i].forward[i] = target.forward[i]   # unlink the target at this level

    def _random_level(self) -> int:
        new_level = 1                                                                   # every node exists at least at level 1
        while random.random() < 0.5 and new_level < SkipListLeaderboard.MAX_LEVEL:          # coin flip decides whether to grow taller
            new_level += 1
        return new_level   # this new node's height


if __name__ == "__main__":
    leaderboard = SkipListLeaderboard()   # a fresh, empty leaderboard

    leaderboard.update_score("Alice", 100)   # Alice joins with 100
    leaderboard.update_score("Bob", 85)         # Bob joins with 85
    leaderboard.update_score("Carol", 95)         # Carol joins with 95

    print(f"Alice's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Alice')}")   # expect 1, highest score
    print(f"Carol's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Carol')}")   # expect 2
    print(f"Bob's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Bob')}")         # expect 3, lowest score

    leaderboard.update_score("Bob", 105)   # Bob has a great match and takes the lead
    print("After Bob's update to 105:")
    print(f"Bob's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Bob')}")         # expect 1, now the highest
    print(f"Alice's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Alice')}")   # expect 2, pushed down one
    print(f"Carol's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Carol')}")   # expect 3, pushed down one

    leaderboard.update_score("Dave", 95)   # Dave ties Carol's score of 95 exactly
    print("After Dave ties Carol's score of 95:")
    print(f"Carol's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Carol')}")   # expect 3, alphabetically before Dave
    print(f"Dave's rank: {leaderboard.get_rank('Dave')}")         # expect 4, tie broken alphabetically
    tie_ok = leaderboard.get_rank("Carol") < leaderboard.get_rank("Dave")
    print(f"Tie correctly broken with Carol ahead of Dave: {str(tie_ok).lower()}")

items: Architecture: one skip-list-backed primary per leaderboard, replicated asynchronously for read scaling, with scaling handled by adding independent leaderboards rather than sharding one.
Capacity: a hundred million players in one leaderboard fitting in about ten gigabytes of memory, fifty thousand score updates per second at peak, and read traffic far exceeding write traffic.
The core data structure: a skip list, giving roughly logarithmic time updates and rank lookups, walked through with a real, working implementation.
Database: a durable snapshot and append log backing the live in-memory structure, mirroring the same event-sourced idea used elsewhere in this project.
End-to-end workflows: score submission and nearby-rank lookup, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Trade-offs: exact skip-list ranking versus a naive full re-sort versus an approximate bucketed-percentile approach, compared directly on rank cost, update cost, and where each breaks down.
Production considerations: deliberate, monitored primary promotion during planned maintenance, and load testing that specifically respects this system's heavily read-skewed traffic shape.
